newsitem.title: GUAM: U.S. experts say too early for Korean crash cause.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts say too early for Korean crash cause.

text.p: U.S. safety investigators searched through wreckage of a Korean Air Lines jumbo jetliner on Thursday and said it was too early to determine what caused the crash that killed all but 27 of 254 people aboard.

"It is really too early to speculate the cause of this accident," George Black, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and chairman of the committee investigating the crash, told a news conference.

U.S. military officials halted a search for bodies in the wreckage to allow the crash experts to look for clues. "There could be about 100 more bodies in the fuselage. But the military is waiting for the National Transportation Safety Board personnel to arrive on the scene, who then will take over from us," U.S. Air Force Colonel Al Riggle told reporters. Riggle said the wreckage, strewn over a wide stretch of mainly scrub brush and razor-sharp tropical grasses, had finally stopped smouldering.
But temperatures hovering around 35 Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) kept conditions difficult for 300 military personnel at the scene.
The NTSB's Black discounted speculation the crash was related to the lack of a key navigation facility that had been shut down for maintenance since last month.
"That was fairly well-known information that the Glidescope indicator was out," he said.
The Glidescope indicator is a device common in most airports of the world that guides an aircraft in for a night landing. Without the Glidescope, pilots use radar beacons for an instrumental landing.
Black said it was common for NTSB probes to take more than a year.
The flight data and voice recorders arrived in Washington on Wednesday night and work on deciphering the information began immediately, according to a spokesman for the NTSB.
Military officials gave up hope on Wednesday evening of finding any more survivors amid the wreckage.
Late on Thursday, officials said there were now just 27 survivors after three injured people died in hospital. Altogether 74 people were confirmed dead and 153 remained missing.
One of the survivors is Rika Matsuda, an 11-year-old Japanese girl plucked from the burning wreckage by Guam Governor Carl Gutierrez.
Rika, clutching a toy animal, appeared at a news conference on Thursday with the governor and her father, who had flown in from Japan.
"I thank the governor, the rescue workers, the hospital officials and the people of Guam," the father said. "Thanks to all of you, it seems Rika is alright now."
Rika's mother was believed to have perished in the flames which engulfed the plane.

The Boeing 747 slammed into a hillside as it approached the airport during a torrential downpour in the early hours of Wednesday. Flight 801 from Seoul was carrying 231 passengers and 23 crew, including dozens of vacationers and several South Korean politicians.
At Guam's airport a few kilometres (miles) away, hysterical mourners mixed with holidaymakers as hundreds of Koreans arrived to claim the bodies of loved ones.
Some 250 South Koreans who reached the island 24 hours after the crash included wailing old women in black mourning garb, stone-faced KAL officials and a group of Seoul nurses flown in to help.
"What will I do now? How will I live on?" shrieked an elderly Korean woman, who nearly collapsed in the airport arrival lounge.
